Guard against typosquatting and dependency confusion by using trusted registries and scoped names.
eg: Most application code is third-party code. Inventory and updating of dependencies is a security task.

term: Tool sets and build toolchain security
def: Compilers, build servers, linters, scanners and package managers are part of the trusted base. Protect them with signed tools, hardened and ephemeral build agents, restricted credentials, isolated networks and reproducible builds. The SLSA framework describes increasing levels of build integrity and provenance for artifacts.
eg: If the toolchain is compromised, every product built with it is compromised.

def: Developer tools run with the developer's privileges. Limit and review extensions and plugins, keep secrets out of project files with pre-commit secret scanning, enable security linting in the editor, use managed, patched workstations or controlled remote development environments, and review code suggested by AI assistants as untrusted input.
eg: A malicious plugin or leaked token on one developer machine can reach source code and pipelines.

def: Software runs in processes, containers, virtual machines, managed runtimes or serverless platforms, each with its own isolation. Apply least privilege to the runtime identity, restrict system calls and file access, set resource limits, use read-only file systems, keep base images patched and consider runtime protection that detects exploitation as it happens.
eg: Isolation limits blast radius; it does not fix a vulnerable application.

term: Software configuration management and version control
def: Software configuration management identifies configuration items (source, build files, documentation), places them under version control, records baselines for each release, controls branches and merges, and audits that deployed software matches the approved baseline. It supports traceability, rollback and reproducible builds.
eg: If you cannot say exactly which version and configuration is in production, you cannot patch or investigate it reliably.

def: Protect repositories with single sign-on and MFA, least-privilege roles, branch protection that requires review and passing checks, signed commits or tags, secret scanning, dependency alerts, audit logs and backups. Private repositories must stay private, and pipeline tokens must be scoped and rotated.
eg: The repository is the crown jewel of a software company. Treat write access like production access.

term: Auditing and logging of software changes
def: Record who changed what, when and why: commit history linked to change tickets, signed commits, review approvals, pipeline logs and deployment records, stored where developers cannot alter them. This supports accountability, investigation of malicious changes and compliance evidence.
eg: Linking each production change to an approved ticket and review is the standard evidence auditors look for.

term: Risk analysis and mitigation in software development
def: Assess risk at requirements and design with threat modeling and rating methods (CVSS, DREAD or qualitative scales), then decide to mitigate, transfer, avoid or accept, record the decision with an owner and trace each mitigation to a requirement and a test. Residual risk is formally accepted before release.
eg: Risk acceptance belongs to the business owner, not the developer.

term: Commercial, open-source and third-party software compared
def: Commercial off-the-shelf software comes with vendor support, contracts and patches but little visibility into the code. Open source offers transparency and flexibility but no guaranteed support, and its licenses (permissive or copyleft) bring obligations. Third-party and outsourced code may bring both. All must be inventoried, assessed and kept patched.
eg: Open source is not automatically more secure ("many eyes" is not a control); check maintenance activity and known vulnerabilities.

term: Managed services and cloud services in software acquisition
def: With managed services and enterprise applications the provider runs the platform, but the customer still owns configuration, identities, data and customizations, whether the service is SaaS, PaaS or IaaS. Before buying, assess the provider with SOC 2 or ISO reports and contract terms such as security duties, breach notification, audit rights, data location and exit.
eg: Customizations and integrations (custom code, APIs, connectors) are the customer's security responsibility even in SaaS.

term: Security terms for software acquisition contracts
def: Contracts should require security requirements and testing evidence, vulnerability and patch timelines, breach notification, a software bill of materials, rights to audit or review assessments, secure development practices, data handling and location terms, source code escrow where appropriate, exit support and liability.
eg: Security obligations not written into the contract are very hard to enforce later.

term: NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF, SP 800-218)
def: The SSDF organizes secure development practices into four groups: Prepare the Organization (people, processes, tools), Protect the Software (code and build integrity), Produce Well-Secured Software (design, review, testing, secure defaults) and Respond to Vulnerabilities (find, fix, and learn). Version 1.1 is the current final release (a version 1.2 draft was issued for comment in December 2025) and underpins US federal supplier attestation.

Version 1.1 is the current final release (a version 1.2 draft was issued for comment in December 2025) and underpins US federal supplier attestation.
eg: The four groups are PO, PS, PW and RV; know the verbs: prepare, protect, produce, respond.

def: Useful measures include vulnerability density by severity, time to fix, escape rate (flaws found after release), scan and test coverage, percentage of components with an SBOM, recurring weakness types, and results of penetration tests and bug reports. Review trends, set thresholds for release and feed lessons back into training and design.
eg: Measure outcomes: fewer escaped flaws and faster fixes matter more than the number of scans run.

term: Low-code, no-code and AI-assisted development risks
def: Low-code and no-code platforms let non-developers build applications, which can create shadow IT with over-shared data, insecure connectors and no testing. AI coding assistants can suggest insecure code, leak code to external services and introduce unvetted dependencies. Govern both with approved platforms, data rules, review, scanning and training.
eg: Treat generated or citizen-built code like any other code: review, test and own it.

term: Prompt injection and LLM-integrated application security
def: In prompt injection, attacker-supplied text (direct, or hidden in documents and web pages the model reads) overrides intended instructions. Applications that connect a language model to tools and data must limit its permissions, validate and filter outputs, separate untrusted content, require human approval for sensitive actions and log activity. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications lists this first.
eg: The model should be treated as an untrusted component with access only to what it needs.

def: Use parameterized queries or a vetted object-relational mapper instead of building SQL from strings, give the application a least-privilege database account, avoid dynamic SQL in stored procedures, keep credentials in a secrets manager and encrypt connections and sensitive columns. Separate read and write accounts where useful.
eg: The database account the application uses should never be a database administrator.
